# Unit 1: Further on Sets
## 1.1 Sets and Elements
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 1 of 363 (PDF Page 13) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (1.1 Sets and Elements):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 2):** Topic 1.1: Sets and Elements
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 1.1: Sets and Elements
> • Set Notations & Representations: Roster method lists elements inside braces A = {1, 2, 3}. Set-builder notation specifies defining property A = {x ∈ ℝ | P(x)}. Empty set (Ø or {}) contains no elements. Universal set (U) contains all discussion elements.
> • Fundamental Set Operations: Union (A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}); Intersection (A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}); Set Difference (A \ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}); Absolute Complement (A' = U \ A).
> • De Morgan's Laws: 1) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'; 2) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'. Complement of union equals intersection of complements.
> • Venn Diagrams & Inclusion-Exclusion Principle: Visualizing set relations using overlapping region circles. Cardinality formula for two sets: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Set theory provides the foundational language for all modern mathematics. Sets categorize mathematical objects, while set operations and Venn diagrams formalize logical inclusion, exclusion, and classification.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Topic 1.1: Sets and Elements

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Empty set Ø is a subset of every set (Ø ⊆ A); Ø ≠ {0} and Ø ≠ {Ø}.
- **Key Principle**: De Morgan's laws swap union and intersection operators when distributing prime complement.
- **Key Principle**: Venn diagrams convert word problems into algebraic equations using n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Venn Diagram Representation: [Circle A] OVERLAPS [Circle B]. Middle Region = A ∩ B; Total Outer Area = A ∪ B; Outside both circles = (A ∪ B)'.
```

b. Collection of beautiful girls in your class.

c. Collection of consonants of the English alphabet.

d. Collection of hardworking teachers in a school.

*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 3 of 363 (PDF Page 15) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 1.1: Sets and Elements
> • Set Notations & Representations: Roster method lists elements inside braces A = {1, 2, 3}. Set-builder notation specifies defining property A = {x ∈ ℝ | P(x)}. Empty set (Ø or {}) contains no elements. Universal set (U) contains all discussion elements.
> • Fundamental Set Operations: Union (A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}); Intersection (A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}); Set Difference (A \ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}); Absolute Complement (A' = U \ A).
> • De Morgan's Laws: 1) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'; 2) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'. Complement of union equals intersection of complements.

If 𝑎 is an element of set 𝐴, we say "𝑎 belongs to 𝐴". The Greek symbol ∈ (epsilon) is

used to denote the phrase "belongs to". Thus, we write 𝒂 ∈ 𝑨 if 𝑎 is a member of set

𝐴. If 𝑏 is not an element of set 𝐴, we write 𝒃 ∉ 𝑨 and read as "𝑏 does not belong to

set 𝐴" or "𝑏 is not a member of set A".

> 🖼️ **Figure 1.1**

> *(Original textbook diagram/illustration — View crisp illustration in the "Exact Page" tab)*

a. The set of students in your class is a well-defined set since the elements of the set

are clearly known.

because it is difficult to list members of the set.

but 𝑏 ∉ 𝐺.

blank spaces.

a. 4 ∈ 𝐴 b. 5 ∉ 𝐴, c. −2 ∉ 𝐴, d. 0 ∉ 𝐴.

i) Sets are usually denoted by capital letters like 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶, 𝑋, 𝑌, 𝑍, etc.

### 1.2 Set Description

Sets can be described in the following ways.

i) Verbal method (Statement form)

In this method, the well-defined description of the elements of the set is written in an

ordinary English language statement form (in words).

a. The set of whole numbers greater than 1 and less than 20.

b. The set of students in this mathematics class.

ii) Listing Methods

a) Complete listing method (Roster Method)

In this method, all elements of the set are completely listed. The elements are

separated by commas and are enclosed within set braces, { }.

a. The set of all even positive integers less than 7 is described in complete listing

method as {2, 4, 6}.

b. The set of all vowel letters in the English alphabet is described in complete listing

method as {𝑎, 𝑒, 𝑖, 𝑜, 𝑢 }.

Let 𝐴 = {1, 2, 3, 4} and 𝐵 = {4, 3, 2, 1}. Then, 𝐴 = 𝐵. Set 𝐴 and set 𝐵 are equal.
Equivalent Sets
Consider two sets 𝐴 = {1, 2, 3, 4} and 𝐵 = {Red, Blue, Green, Black}.
In set 𝐴 there are four elements and in set 𝐵 also there are four elements. Therefore,
set 𝐴 and set 𝐵 are equivalent.
Universal Set (∪)
Let set 𝐴 = {2, 4, 6, . . . } and 𝐵 = {1, 3, 5, . . . }. The universal set U consists of all
natural numbers, such that 𝑈 = {1, 2, 3, 4, . . . }. Therefore, as we know all even and
odd numbers are part of natural numbers. Hence, set U has all the elements of set A
and set B.

between the two sets. This is written mathematically as 𝐴 ↔ 𝐵 (or 𝐴~𝐵).
Observe that two finite sets 𝐴 and 𝐵 are equivalent, if and only if they have equal
number of elements and we write mathematically this as 𝑛 ሺ𝐴ሻ = 𝑛 ሺ𝐵ሻ.

# Unit 1: Further on Sets
## 1.3 The Notion of Sets
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 10 of 363 (PDF Page 22) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (1.3 The Notion of Sets):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 7):** Topic 1.3: The Notion of Sets
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 1.3: The Notion of Sets
> • Set Notations & Representations: Roster method lists elements inside braces A = {1, 2, 3}. Set-builder notation specifies defining property A = {x ∈ ℝ | P(x)}. Empty set (Ø or {}) contains no elements. Universal set (U) contains all discussion elements.
> • Fundamental Set Operations: Union (A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}); Intersection (A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}); Set Difference (A \ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}); Absolute Complement (A' = U \ A).
> • De Morgan's Laws: 1) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'; 2) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'. Complement of union equals intersection of complements.
> • Venn Diagrams & Inclusion-Exclusion Principle: Visualizing set relations using overlapping region circles. Cardinality formula for two sets: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

---

Subset (⊆)

Let 𝐴 = {1, 2, 3} and 𝐵 = {1, 2, 3, 4} be sets. Here, set 𝐴 is a subset of set 𝐵,

or 𝐴 ⊆ 𝐵, since all members of set 𝐴 are found in set 𝐵.

In the above set 𝐴, find all subsets of the set. How many subsets does set 𝐴 have?

Solution:

The subsets of set 𝐴 are {1}, {2}, {3}, {1, 2}, {2, 3}, {1, 3}, {1, 2, 3}, { }. The number of

subsets of set 𝐴 is 8.

In the above Example 3. b, 𝑛ሺ𝐴ሻ = 3. Then, the number of subsets is 23 = 8.

Proper Subset (⊂)

Definition 1.5

Set 𝐴 is said to be a subset of set 𝐵 if every

element of 𝐴 is also an element of 𝐵. Figure

### 1.3 shows this relationship. Mathematically,

we write this as 𝑨 ⊆ 𝑩 . If set 𝐴 is not a

subset of set 𝐵, then it is written as 𝐴 ⊈ 𝐵.

Example 4

ii) Empty set is a subset of every set.

Note

Definition 1.6

If 𝐴 ⊆ 𝐵 and 𝐴 ≠ 𝐵, then 𝐴 is called the proper subset of set 𝐵 and it can be

written as 𝐴 ⊂ 𝐵.

Set theory provides the foundational language for all modern mathematics. Sets categorize mathematical objects, while set operations and Venn diagrams formalize logical inclusion, exclusion, and classification.

- **Key Principle**: Empty set Ø is a subset of every set (Ø ⊆ A); Ø ≠ {0} and Ø ≠ {Ø}.
- **Key Principle**: De Morgan's laws swap union and intersection operators when distributing prime complement.
- **Key Principle**: Venn diagrams convert word problems into algebraic equations using n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

Solution:
𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 = {𝑥 | 𝑥 is a positive integer that is either even or a multiple of 3}

𝐴 ∩ 𝐵 = {𝑥 | 𝑥 is a positive integer that is both even and a multiple of 3}

2. Let 𝐴 be the set of positive odd integers less than 10 and 𝐵 is the set of positive
multiples of 5 less than or equal to 20. Find a) 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵, b) 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵.

## Unit 1: Further on Sets

Complement of sets

a. Let 𝑈 = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} and 𝐴 = {3, 4}. Then, 𝐴′ = {0, 1, 2}.

Let 𝑈 = {1, 2, 3, … , 10} be a universal set,

𝐴 = {𝑥 | 𝑥 is a positive factor of 10 in 𝑈} and

𝐵 = {𝑥 | 𝑥 is an odd integer in 𝑈} be sets.

a. Find 𝐴′ and 𝐵′.

b. Find ሺ𝐴 ∪ 𝐵ሻ′ and 𝐴′ ∩ 𝐵′. What do you observe from the answers?

Solution:

a. 𝐴 = {1, 2, 5, 10}, 𝐵 = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, Thus,

𝐴′ = {3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9}, 𝐵′ = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}.

b. First, we find 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵. Hence, 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 = {1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9,10} and

ሺ𝐴 ∪ 𝐵ሻ′ = {4, 6, 8}.

On the other hand, from 𝐴′ and 𝐵′ , we obtain 𝐴′ ∩ 𝐵′ = {4, 6, 8} . Hence, we

immediately observe ሺ𝐴 ∪ 𝐵ሻ′ = 𝐴′ ∩ 𝐵′.

In general, for any two sets 𝐴 and 𝐵 , ሺ𝐴 ∪ 𝐵ሻ′ = 𝐴′ ∩ 𝐵′. It is called the first

statement of De Morgan's law.

Definition 1.9

Let 𝐴 be a subset of a universal set 𝑈. The

absolute complement (or simply complement)

of 𝐴, which is denoted by 𝑨′, is defined as the

set of all elements of 𝑈 that are not in 𝐴. We

write this mathematically as

𝐴′ = {𝑥: 𝑥 ∈ 𝑈 and 𝑥 ∉ 𝐴}.

## 1.4 Operations on Sets
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 17 of 363 (PDF Page 29) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (1.4 Operations on Sets):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 12):** Topic 1.4: Operations on Sets
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 1.4: Operations on Sets
> • Set Notations & Representations: Roster method lists elements inside braces A = {1, 2, 3}. Set-builder notation specifies defining property A = {x ∈ ℝ | P(x)}. Empty set (Ø or {}) contains no elements. Universal set (U) contains all discussion elements.
> • Fundamental Set Operations: Union (A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B}); Intersection (A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}); Set Difference (A \ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B}); Absolute Complement (A' = U \ A).
> • De Morgan's Laws: 1) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'; 2) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'. Complement of union equals intersection of complements.
> • Venn Diagrams & Inclusion-Exclusion Principle: Visualizing set relations using overlapping region circles. Cardinality formula for two sets: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 17 — Structured Curriculum Text

## Unit 1: Further on Sets

If sets 𝐴 = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} and 𝐵 = {3, 4}, then 𝐴 − 𝐵 or 𝐴\𝐵 = {0, 1, 2}.

Let 𝑈 be a universal set of the set of one-digit numbers, 𝐴 be the set of even

numbers, 𝐵 be the set of prime numbers less than 10. Find the following:

a. 𝐴 − 𝐵 or 𝐴\𝐵 b. 𝐵 − 𝐴 or 𝐵\𝐴

c. 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 d. 𝑈 − ሺ𝐴 ∪ 𝐵ሻ or 𝑈\ሺ𝐴 ∪ 𝐵ሻ

Solution:

Here, 𝐴 = {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}, 𝐵 = {2, 3, 5, 7}. Then,

we illustrate the sets using a Venn diagram as

follows. From the Venn diagram we observe:

a. 𝐴 − 𝐵 = {0, 4, 6, 8}

b. 𝐵 − 𝐴 = {3 ,5, 7}

c. 𝐴 ∪ 𝐵 = {0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}

d. 𝑈 − ሺ𝐴 ∪ 𝐵ሻ = {1, 9}

For the same sets in Example 2, find the following. What can you say from Example

2 a. and b.? What about d. and Example 2, a.?

a. 𝐴′ b. 𝑈 − 𝐴

c. 𝐵′ d. 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵′

Solution:

a. 𝐴′ = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9} b. 𝑈 − 𝐴 = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}

c. 𝐵′ = {0, 1, 4, 6, 8, 9} d. 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵′ = {0, 4, 6, 8}

From a. and b., we can say, 𝐴′ = 𝑈 − 𝐴. From d. and Example 2, a., we can say,

𝐴 − 𝐵 = 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵′.

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Set theory provides the foundational language for all modern mathematics. Sets categorize mathematical objects, while set operations and Venn diagrams formalize logical inclusion, exclusion, and classification.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Topic 1.4: Operations on Sets

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Empty set Ø is a subset of every set (Ø ⊆ A); Ø ≠ {0} and Ø ≠ {Ø}.
- **Key Principle**: De Morgan's laws swap union and intersection operators when distributing prime complement.
- **Key Principle**: Venn diagrams convert word problems into algebraic equations using n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Venn Diagram Representation: [Circle A] OVERLAPS [Circle B]. Middle Region = A ∩ B; Total Outer Area = A ∪ B; Outside both circles = (A ∪ B)'.
```

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Set theory algorithms structure demographic censuses by the Ethiopian Central Statistics Agency and query database records in national banking networks.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
Very high frequency in EUEE: applying De Morgan's laws to simplify set expressions like (A' ∩ B')' = A ∪ B, and solving two-set word problems.

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
Master set operations (union, intersection, complement) and apply De Morgan's laws (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and inclusion-exclusion n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

Summary and Review Exercise

1. A set is a collection of well-defined objects or elements. When we say a set is

well-defined, we mean that given an object we are able to determine whether the

object is in the set or not.

2. Sets can be described in the following ways:

Verbal method (Statement form)

In this method, the well-defined description of the elements of the set is written

in an ordinary English language statement form (in words).

Complete listing method (Roster Method)

In this method all the elements of the sets are completely listed. The elements

are separated by commas and are enclosed within set brace, { }.

Partial listing method

We use this method, if listing of all elements of a set is difficult or impossible

but the elements can be indicated clearly by listing a few of them that fully

describe the set.

Set builder method (Method of defining property)

The set-builder method is described by a property that its member must satisfy.

This is the method of writing the condition to be satisfied by a set or property of

a set.

3. A set which does not contain any element is called an empty set, void set or null

set. The empty set is denoted mathematically by the symbol {} or ∅.

4. Two sets A and B are said to be equal if and only if they have exactly same or

identical elements. Mathematically, we write this as 𝐴 = 𝐵.

5. Set 𝐴 is said to be a subset of set 𝐵 if every element of 𝐴 is also an element of

𝐵. Mathematically, we write this as 𝐴 ⊆ 𝐵.

• Any set is a subset to itself.

• Empty set is a sub set of every set.

7. Suppose the universal set 𝑈 be the set of one-digit numbers, and
set 𝐴 = {𝑥 | 𝑥 is an even natural number less than or equal to 9 }.
Describe each set by complete listing method:
a. 𝐴′
b. 𝐴 ∩ 𝐴′
c. 𝐴 ∪ 𝐴′
d. (𝐴′)′
e. 𝜙 \ 𝑈
f. 𝜙′
g. 𝑈′
8. Let 𝑈 = {1, 2, 3, 4, … … . ,10}, 𝐴 = {1, 3, 5, 7}, 𝐵 = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Evaluate
𝑈\(𝐴∆𝐵).
9. Consider a universal set 𝑈 = {1, 2, 3, . . . , 14}, 𝐴 = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11},
𝐵 = {2, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11}. Then, which one of the following is true?
A. (𝐴 ∪ 𝐵)′ = {1, 4, 6, 12, 13, 14}
B. 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵 = 𝐴′ ∪ 𝐵′
C. 𝐴∆𝐵 = (𝐴 ∩ 𝐵)′
D. 𝐴\𝐵 = {3, 5, 7}
E. None

of the two sets are integers. If 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵 = {4, 7}, then find a and b. In addition,
find 𝐴 ⋃ 𝐵.
11. In a survey of 200 students in Motta Secondary School, 90 students are
members of Nature club, 31 students are members of Mini-media club, 21
students are members of both clubs. Answer the following questions.
a. How many students are members of either of the clubs?
b. How many students are not members of either of the clubs?
25

> • Rational vs. Irrational Numbers: Rational numbers can be written as a/b (b ≠ 0) with terminating or repeating decimals. Irrational numbers cannot be expressed as a fraction and have non-terminating, non-repeating decimals (e.g. √2, π, e).
> • Proof of Irrationality of √2: By contradiction: assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms. 2b² = a² ⇒ a is even ⇒ 4k² = 2b² ⇒ b is even. Contradicts assumption of lowest terms.
> • Radical Algebraic Rules: √(ab) = √a·√b and √(a/b) = √a/√b for a, b ≥ 0. Rationalizing denominators: multiply by conjugate (√a - √b) / (√a - √b) to eliminate surds from denominator.
> • Absolute Value Properties: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and -x if x < 0. Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|. Distance between points a and b is |a - b|.

Is 18 a prime number or a composite number? Why?

Find a prime number(s) greater than 50 and less than 55.

The natural numbers greater than 50 and less than 55 are 51, 52, 53 and 54.

52 = 2 × 26, so that 2 and 26 are factors of 52, and

54 = 2 × 27, hence 2 and 27 are factors of 54. Therefore, these three numbers are

composite numbers. But 53 = 1 × 53. Hence, 1 and 53 are the only factors of 53 so

that 53 is a prime number. Therefore, 53 is a prime number greater than 50 and less

than 55.

and 56. The greatest one from these common

diagram.

2 = 2.55. Again take the average of 3.1 and 4.2, that is

3.1+4.2

2 = 3.65. These numbers 2.55 and 3.65 are also between 2 and 4.2.

Rounding off is a type of estimation. Estimation is used in everyday life and also in

digits that are on the right hand side of the requested rounding digit become

zero.

and subtract this value (value in step2) from the given value to obtain the

lower bound.

and the

1. First let us find a number between 1 and 10, that is a number which has 1

digit in front of the decimal point from the given number. The number is

1.8567.

Definition 2.15

A number is said to be in scientific notation (or standard notation) if it is written

as a product of the form 𝑎 × 10𝑛 where 1 ≤ 𝑎 < 10 and 𝑛 is an integer.

### 📋 Activity 3.1 leads you to revise the rules used to solve linear equations that you

learned in the previous grades.

For solving a linear equation in one variable, the following steps are

followed:

Step 1: Use LCM (Least Common Multiple) to clear the fractions if any.

Step 2: Simplify both sides of the equation.

Step 3: Isolate the variable.

Step 4: Verify your answer.

Solve for 𝑥, if

a. 𝑥 + 2 = 0 b. 3𝑥 + 4 = 10

Solution:

a. Add −2 on both sides to isolate the variable 𝑥.

𝑥 + 2 + ሺ−2ሻ = 0 + ሺ−2ሻ

𝑥 = −2.

b. Similarly, 3𝑥 + 4 − 4 = 10 − 4

3𝑥 = 6

𝑥 = 6

3 = 2. Hence, 𝑥 = 2

Definition 3.1

When an equation in one variable has exponent equal to 1, it is said to be a linear

equation in one variable. It is of the form 𝑎𝑥 + 𝑏 = 0, where 𝑥 is the variable,

and 𝑎 and 𝑏 are real coefficients and 𝑎 ≠ 0. This equation has only one solution.

substitution

−3𝑥 = −24

𝑥 = 8

Now, we substitute 𝑥 = 8 into the first equation or second equation and solve for y.

−8 + 𝑦 = −5

### 3.2.2 Solving systems of linear equations in two

variables by substitution

One of the methods of solving a system of linear equations is substitution method.

The method involves solving one of the equations in terms of the other variable and

then substitute the result into the other equation to solve the second variable.

Steps in solving systems of linear equations in two variables by

substitution

Step 1. Solve one of the two equations for one of the variables in terms of the other.

Step 2. Substitute the expression for this variable into the second equation, then solve

for the remaining variable.

Step 3. Substitute that solution into either of the original equations to find the value

of the first variable. If possible, write the solution as an ordered pair.

Step 4. Check the solution in both equations.

Graphical method is one of the methods of solving systems of linear equations.

Solving a linear system in two variables by graphing works well when the solution

consists of integer values, but if our solution contains decimals or fractions, it is not

the most precise method. For a system of linear equations in two variables, we can

determine both the type of system and the solution by graphing the system of

equations on the same set of axes.

To solve systems of linear equations using graphs, use the following steps:

Step 1. Graph the first equation.

Step 2. Graph the second equation using the same coordinate system.

Step 3. Determine whether the lines intersect, are parallel, or are the same line.

determine both the type of system and the solution by graphing the system of

equations on the same set of axes.

Step 2. Graph the second equation using the same coordinate system.

intersection.

line. Every point on the line represents a coordinate pair that satisfies the system.

> • Linear Equations & Inequalities in 1 Variable: Form ax + b = 0 (solution x = -b/a). Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number REVERSES the inequality sign (e.g., -2x < 6 ⟹ x > -3). Solution sets expressed on real line or in interval notation.
> • Systems of 2-Variable Linear Equations: ax + by = c and dx + ey = f. Solution methods: 1) Substitution; 2) Elimination; 3) Graphical intersection point (x, y). Consistent unique solution (intersecting lines), inconsistent no solution (parallel lines), dependent infinite solutions (coincident lines).
> • Quadratic Equations: Standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0). Methods: Factoring, completing the square, and Quadratic Formula: x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / (2a).

An object dropped from a height of 600m has a height, ℎ, in meter after 𝑡 seconds

We are asked two things. First, we will solve the height equation for 𝑡, and then we

ℎ = 600 − 16𝑡2

𝑡2 = 600−ℎ

𝑡 = √600−ℎ

16 = ξ600−ℎ

We want time to be only positive since we are talking about a measurable quantity,

so we will restrict our answers to just 𝑡 = ξ600−ℎ

We want to know at what time the height will be 200𝑚. So we can substitute 200

for ℎ.

𝑡 = ξ600−200

4 = ξ400

4 = 20

4 = 5

Therefore, it takes 5 seconds for the object to be at the height of 200𝑚.

velocity of 48 meters per second. Its height, h, in meter above the ground is modeled

by the equation ℎ = −16𝑡2 + 𝑣0𝑡 + 64 where 𝑡 > 0 is the time in second, since the

projectile was launched and v0 is the initial velocity. How long was the projectile in

the air?

# Unit 4: Solving Inequalities
## 4.1 Revision on Linear Inequalities in One Variable
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 153 of 363 (PDF Page 165) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (4.1 Revision on Linear Inequalities in One Variable):**

> • Linear Equations & Inequalities in 1 Variable: Form ax + b = 0 (solution x = -b/a). Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number REVERSES the inequality sign (e.g., -2x < 6 ⟹ x > -3). Solution sets expressed on real line or in interval notation.
> • Systems of 2-Variable Linear Equations: ax + by = c and dx + ey = f. Solution methods: 1) Substitution; 2) Elimination; 3) Graphical intersection point (x, y). Consistent unique solution (intersecting lines), inconsistent no solution (parallel lines), dependent infinite solutions (coincident lines).
> • Quadratic Equations: Standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0). Methods: Factoring, completing the square, and Quadratic Formula: x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / (2a).

Important procedures in solving inequalities in two variables

graphically

To solve an inequality in two variables graphically, first sketch the corresponding

equations on the same xy-plane. This graph is the boundary line (or curve); since all

points that make the inequality true lie on one side or the other of the line. Before

graphing the equations, decide whether the line or curve is part of the solution or not,

that is, whether it is solid or dashed.

If the inequality symbol is either ≤ or ≥, then the points on the boundary line are

solutions to the inequality and the line must be solid. If the symbol is either < or >,

then the points on the boundary line are not solutions to the inequality and the line is

dashed.

> • Number System Hierarchy: ℕ (Natural) ⊂ 𝕎 (Whole) ⊂ ℤ (Integers) ⊂ ℚ (Rationals) ⊂ ℝ (Real Numbers). Complex numbers ℂ contain all real and imaginary roots.
> • Rational vs. Irrational Numbers: Rational numbers can be written as a/b (b ≠ 0) with terminating or repeating decimals. Irrational numbers cannot be expressed as a fraction and have non-terminating, non-repeating decimals (e.g. √2, π, e).
> • Proof of Irrationality of √2: By contradiction: assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms. 2b² = a² ⇒ a is even ⇒ 4k² = 2b² ⇒ b is even. Contradicts assumption of lowest terms.
> • Radical Algebraic Rules: √(ab) = √a·√b and √(a/b) = √a/√b for a, b ≥ 0. Rationalizing denominators: multiply by conjugate (√a - √b) / (√a - √b) to eliminate surds from denominator.
> • Absolute Value Properties: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and -x if x < 0. Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|. Distance between points a and b is |a - b|.

*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 167 of 363 (PDF Page 179) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (4.3 Inequalities Involving Absolute Value):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 166):** Topic 4.3: Inequalities Involving Absolute Value
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 4.3: Inequalities Involving Absolute Value
> • Number System Hierarchy: ℕ (Natural) ⊂ 𝕎 (Whole) ⊂ ℤ (Integers) ⊂ ℚ (Rationals) ⊂ ℝ (Real Numbers). Complex numbers ℂ contain all real and imaginary roots.
> • Rational vs. Irrational Numbers: Rational numbers can be written as a/b (b ≠ 0) with terminating or repeating decimals. Irrational numbers cannot be expressed as a fraction and have non-terminating, non-repeating decimals (e.g. √2, π, e).
> • Proof of Irrationality of √2: By contradiction: assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms. 2b² = a² ⇒ a is even ⇒ 4k² = 2b² ⇒ b is even. Contradicts assumption of lowest terms.
> • Radical Algebraic Rules: √(ab) = √a·√b and √(a/b) = √a/√b for a, b ≥ 0. Rationalizing denominators: multiply by conjugate (√a - √b) / (√a - √b) to eliminate surds from denominator.
> • Absolute Value Properties: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and -x if x < 0. Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|. Distance between points a and b is |a - b|.

b. |𝑥| > 1 are the numbers that satisfy 𝑥 < −1 or 𝑥 > 1.

The solutions of |𝑘| < 𝑐 are the numbers that satisfy −𝑐 < 𝑘 < 𝑐

Solve the absolute value inequality |𝑥 + 2| < 4.

The solutions of |𝑘| < 𝑐 are the numbers that satisfy −𝑐 < 𝑘 < 𝑐.

Hence, |𝑥 + 2| < 4

> • Number System Hierarchy: ℕ (Natural) ⊂ 𝕎 (Whole) ⊂ ℤ (Integers) ⊂ ℚ (Rationals) ⊂ ℝ (Real Numbers). Complex numbers ℂ contain all real and imaginary roots.
> • Rational vs. Irrational Numbers: Rational numbers can be written as a/b (b ≠ 0) with terminating or repeating decimals. Irrational numbers cannot be expressed as a fraction and have non-terminating, non-repeating decimals (e.g. √2, π, e).
> • Proof of Irrationality of √2: By contradiction: assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms. 2b² = a² ⇒ a is even ⇒ 4k² = 2b² ⇒ b is even. Contradicts assumption of lowest terms.
> • Radical Algebraic Rules: √(ab) = √a·√b and √(a/b) = √a/√b for a, b ≥ 0. Rationalizing denominators: multiply by conjugate (√a - √b) / (√a - √b) to eliminate surds from denominator.
> • Absolute Value Properties: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and -x if x < 0. Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|. Distance between points a and b is |a - b|.

Solution:

Therefore, the solution of this quadratic inequality is 𝑥 ≤ −3 or 𝑥 ≥ 4 .

Alternatively, the solution is (−∞, −3] ∪ [4, ∞).

adjacent sides to 90° are equal in length.

we can write a relation using the Pythagoras theorem, that is 𝑏2 + 𝑝2 = ℎ2.

> • Angles & Parallel Lines: Transversal intersecting two parallel lines forms: 1) Corresponding angles (equal); 2) Alternate interior angles (equal); 3) Alternate exterior angles (equal); 4) Consecutive interior angles (supplementary, sum = 180°).

# Unit 5: Introduction to Trigonometry
## 5.2 Trigonometric Ratios
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 191 of 363 (PDF Page 203) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (5.2 Trigonometric Ratios):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 190):** Topic 5.2: Trigonometric Ratios
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 5.2: Trigonometric Ratios
> • Primary Trigonometric Ratios (Right Triangle): sin θ = Opp/Hyp, cos θ = Adj/Hyp, tan θ = Opp/Adj (SOH-CAH-TOA). Reciprocals: csc θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.
> • Unit Circle & Radians: Coordinates of point on unit circle (r = 1): (x, y) = (cos θ, sin θ). Angle conversion: π radians = 180°. Quadrant signs (ASTC rule): All positive in Q1, Sin in Q2, Tan in Q3, Cos in Q4.
> • Fundamental Pythagorean Identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.
> • Addition & Double-Angle Formulas: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B; cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B; sin(2θ) = 2 sin θ cos θ; cos(2θ) = cos²θ - sin²θ = 2cos²θ - 1 = 1 - 2sin²θ.
> • Laws of Sines & Cosines (Any Triangle): Law of Sines: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C = 2R. Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C.

a right-angled triangle can be imagined, as shown in fig 5.4. Can you find out the

height of the building without actually measuring it?

In the above situation, the height can be found by using some mathematical

techniques, which come under a branch of mathematics called 'trigonometry'.

Trigonometry is derived from two Greek words 'trigonon' which means 'triangle' and

'metron' meaning 'measure'. Put together, the words mean "triangle measuring". In

fact, trigonometry is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a

triangle. The earliest known work on trigonometry was recorded in Egypt and

Babylon. Early astronomers used it to find out the distances of the stars and planets

from the Earth. Even today, most of the technologically advanced methods used in

Engineering and Physical Sciences are based on trigonometric concepts.

Now let us define the trigonometric ratio.

Definition 5.2 Trigonometric ratios

The trigonometric ratios of a given angle are defined by the ratios of two sides of

a right-angled triangle. These trigonometric ratios remain unchanged as long as

the angle remains the same, that is, they are independent of the size of the

triangle provided the angle remains the same.

There are six trigonometric ratios. But here we will define only the first three

trigonometric ratios as follows.

Consider the following right-angled triangle as shown in the figure 5.5 below.

# Unit 6: Regular Polygons
## 6.1 Sum of Interior Angles of a Convex Polygon
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 210 of 363 (PDF Page 222) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (6.1 Sum of Interior Angles of a Convex Polygon):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 208):** Topic 6.1: Sum of Interior Angles of a Convex Polygon
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 6.1: Sum of Interior Angles of a Convex Polygon
> • Angles & Parallel Lines: Transversal intersecting two parallel lines forms: 1) Corresponding angles (equal); 2) Alternate interior angles (equal); 3) Alternate exterior angles (equal); 4) Consecutive interior angles (supplementary, sum = 180°).
> • Triangle Congruence & Similarity: Congruent triangles (identical shape and size) criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS. Similar triangles (same shape, proportional sides) criteria: AA, SSS similarity, SAS similarity. Ratio of areas of similar triangles = (scale factor k)².⏹
> • Pythagorean Theorem & Special Right Triangles: In right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c: a² + b² = c². Special triangles: 1) 45°-45°-90° triangle (sides x : x : x√2); 2) 30°-60°-90° triangle (sides x : x√3 : 2x).
> • Quadrilaterals & Polygons: Parallelogram (opposite sides/angles equal, diagonals bisect); Rectangle (right angles, equal diagonals); Rhombus (perpendicular diagonals); Square (all sides/angles equal). Polygon interior angle sum = (n - 2) × 180°; Exterior angle sum = 360°.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 210 — Structured Curriculum Text

## Unit 6: Regular Polygons

> 🖼️ **Figure 6.1 Polygons**

> *(Original textbook diagram/illustration — View crisp illustration in the "Exact Page" tab)*

How many sides and vertices does a hexagon have?

Solution:

A hexagon is a polygon with 6 sides and 6 vertices.

1. How many sides and vertices does a nonagon have?

2. What is the name of a polygon with ten sides?

3. Draw an octagon using a ruler.

4. When a triangle is cut off from a quadrilateral by a straight line which passes

through vertices, write down the names of the possible polygons to be formed.

Example

### ✍️ Exercise 6.1

Definition 6.2

i. A polygon is said to be a convex polygon when the measure of each interior

angle is less than 180 degrees. The vertices of a convex polygon are always

outwards.

ii. A polygon is said to be a concave polygon when there is at least one interior

angle whose measure is more than 180 degrees. The vertices of a concave

polygon present inwards and also outwards.

---

Plane geometry analyzes spatial relationships, angle properties, and structural forms. Congruence and similarity enable indirect distance measurement, while the Pythagorean theorem provides the geometric link between distance and coordinate algebra.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Topic 6.1: Sum of Interior Angles of a Convex Polygon

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Consecutive interior angles along a transversal are supplementary (sum = 180°), NOT equal.
- **Key Principle**: Similarity ratio k implies perimeter ratio k, but area ratio k².
- **Key Principle**: The hypotenuse of a 30°-60°-90° triangle is twice the length of the side opposite the 30° angle.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Parallel Line Transversal: Line L1 ∥ Line L2 crossed by Transversal T ──> Alternate Interior Angles equal (∠3 = ∠6, ∠4 = ∠5); Consecutive Interior sum = 180° (∠3 + ∠5 = 180°).
```

| **Examination Traps** | Very high frequency in EUEE: using similar triangle scale factors to find unknow... | Critical EUEE Target Point |

Structural engineering of bridge girders across the Abay Gorge uses triangular truss stability and Pythagorean diagonal reinforcement.

Parallel line transversals yield equal alternate interior angles; right triangles obey a² + b² = c² and special side ratios (30-60-90 & 45-45-90).

For any 𝑛 -sided polygon, the sum of the measure of exterior angles of the

polygon is 360°.

At each vertex of a polygon, the sum of interior and exterior angles is 180°.

## 6.3 Measures of Each Interior Angle and Exterior Angle of a Regular Polygon
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 222 of 363 (PDF Page 234) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (6.3 Measures of Each Interior Angle and Exterior Angle of a Regular Polygon):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 221):** Topic 6.3: Measures of Each Interior Angle and Exterior Angle of a Regular Polygon
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 6.3: Measures of Each Interior Angle and Exterior Angle of a Regular Polygon
> • Angles & Parallel Lines: Transversal intersecting two parallel lines forms: 1) Corresponding angles (equal); 2) Alternate interior angles (equal); 3) Alternate exterior angles (equal); 4) Consecutive interior angles (supplementary, sum = 180°).
> • Triangle Congruence & Similarity: Congruent triangles (identical shape and size) criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS. Similar triangles (same shape, proportional sides) criteria: AA, SSS similarity, SAS similarity. Ratio of areas of similar triangles = (scale factor k)².⏹
> • Pythagorean Theorem & Special Right Triangles: In right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c: a² + b² = c². Special triangles: 1) 45°-45°-90° triangle (sides x : x : x√2); 2) 30°-60°-90° triangle (sides x : x√3 : 2x).
> • Quadrilaterals & Polygons: Parallelogram (opposite sides/angles equal, diagonals bisect); Rectangle (right angles, equal diagonals); Rhombus (perpendicular diagonals); Square (all sides/angles equal). Polygon interior angle sum = (n - 2) × 180°; Exterior angle sum = 360°.

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 222 — Structured Curriculum Text

## Unit 6: Regular Polygons

For a polygon of the above types, we have the following definition:

For example: -Equilateral triangles and squares

are regular polygons. Students, do you know

honeycomb? We also have such polygons in

our day-to-day life. For instance, figure 6.13

shows a honeycomb which is formed by

honeybees as regular hexagons.

What is the measure of each interior and exterior angle of 𝑛-sided regular

polygon?

For 𝑛-sided polygon, recall that

i. The sum of the measure of interior angles is (𝑛 − 2) × 180°.

ii. The sum of the measure of exterior angles is 360°.

Using this and the definition of regular polygon, the measure of each interior angle of

𝑛-sided regular polygon is determined by

(𝑛−2)×180°

𝑛 (Since a regular polygon is equiangular)

Plane geometry analyzes spatial relationships, angle properties, and structural forms. Congruence and similarity enable indirect distance measurement, while the Pythagorean theorem provides the geometric link between distance and coordinate algebra.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: Consecutive interior angles along a transversal are supplementary (sum = 180°), NOT equal.
- **Key Principle**: Similarity ratio k implies perimeter ratio k, but area ratio k².
- **Key Principle**: The hypotenuse of a 30°-60°-90° triangle is twice the length of the side opposite the 30° angle.

**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Parallel Line Transversal: Line L1 ∥ Line L2 crossed by Transversal T ──> Alternate Interior Angles equal (∠3 = ∠6, ∠4 = ∠5); Consecutive Interior sum = 180° (∠3 + ∠5 = 180°).
```

360°

𝑛 .

then it is said to be symmetric. A symmetrical figure has at least one line of

symmetry. An asymmetrical figure has no line of symmetry.

## Unit 7: Congruency and Similarity

### 7.3.1 AA similarity Theorem

The AA similarity theorem for triangles states that if the two angles of one triangle

are respectively congruent to the two angles of the other, then the triangles are

similar. In short, equiangular triangles are similar. Ideally, the name of this criterion

should then be the AAA (Angle-Angle-Angle) similarity theorem, but we call it

as AA similarity theorem because we need only two pairs of angles to be equal - the

third pair will then automatically be equal by the angle sum property of triangles. The

notation ~ is used to denote similarity.

Consider the following figures, in which ΔABC and ΔDEF are equiangular.

Using the 𝐴𝐴 similarity theorem, we can say that these triangles are similar.

Mathematically, it is written as ∆ABC~∆DEF.

Determine whether or not the following two triangles are similar.

Solution:

Compare the angles to see if we can use the AA similarity theorem. Using triangle

angle sum theorem, m(∠G) = 48o & m(∠M) = 30o. Hence, ∆EFG~∆LMN by AA

similarity theorem.

> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 8.1: Vector and Scalar Quantities
> • Scalars vs Vectors: Scalar quantity has magnitude only (mass, temperature, speed, energy). Vector quantity has BOTH magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force, acceleration). Directed line segment representation AB.
> • 2D Vector Component Form: Vector v in Cartesian plane: v = (v_x, v_y) = v_x i + v_y j, where i = (1, 0) and j = (0, 1) are standard unit vectors along x and y axes. Components: v_x = ||v|| cos θ, v_y = ||v|| sin θ.
> • Magnitude & Direction Angle: Magnitude ||v|| = √(v_x² + v_y²). Direction angle θ = tan⁻¹(v_y / v_x) (quadrant adjusted). Unit vector u in direction of v: u = v / ||v||.
> • Vector Operations: Vector addition u + v = (u_x + v_x, u_y + v_y) (Triangle / Parallelogram Law). Scalar multiplication k·v = (k·v_x, k·v_y). Dot product u · v = u_x v_x + u_y v_y = ||u|| ||v|| cos θ.

# Unit 9: Statistics and Probability
## 9.1 Statistical Data
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 311 of 363 (PDF Page 323) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (9.1 Statistical Data):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 313):** Topic 9.1: Statistical Data
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 9.1: Statistical Data
> • Data Organization & Frequency Distributions: Discrete vs grouped frequency tables. Class intervals, lower/upper class boundaries, class mark (midpoint x = (L + U)/2), and cumulative frequency.
> • Graphical Data Representations: Bar charts (discrete categories, gaps between bars); Histograms (continuous data, bars touch, bar area proportional to frequency); Pie charts (circular sectors, sector angle = (f / N) × 360°).
> • Measures of Central Tendency: 1) Mean x̄ = (Σ x) / n or x̄ = (Σ f·x) / (Σ f); 2) Median: Middle score when data is ordered (for even n, average of two middle terms); 3) Mode: Most frequently occurring score (unimodal, bimodal, or no mode).
> • Basic Probability Concepts: Sample space S (all possible outcomes), Event E (subset of S). Theoretical Probability P(E) = n(E) / n(S) where 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. Complementary Event: P(E') = 1 - P(E).

Statistics and probability provide tools for analyzing data and quantifying uncertainty. Descriptive statistics condense large data sets into summary averages and charts, while probability models chance events.

- **Key Principle**: In a histogram, bars MUST touch because data is continuous; in a bar chart, gaps separate discrete categories.

• Primary data

• Secondary data

• Interviews

• Direct observations

• Questionnaires

Sources of collecting data

Primary Data is a data that has been generated by the researcher himself/herself,

surveys, interviews, experiments, specially designed for understanding and solving

the research problem at hand.

Secondary Data is data used after it is generated by large government institutions,

healthcare facilities, etc. as part of organizational record keeping. The data is then

extracted from more varied data files.

Interview: The main purpose of an interview as a tool of data collection is to gather

data extensively and intensively. Exchanging ideas and experiences, eliciting of

information pertaining to a very wide range of data in which the interviewee may

wish to rehearse his past, define his present and canvass his future possibilities.

Interviews can provide in-depth information pertaining to participants' experiences

and viewpoints of a particular topic. Generally, interview has two types: a) In-depth

and b) focus group.

Direct observations: A technique that involves systematically selecting, watching,

listening, reading, touching, and recording behavior and characteristics of living

things, objects, or phenomena.

# Unit 9: Statistics and Probability
## 9.1 Statistical Data
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 322 of 363 (PDF Page 334) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (9.1 Statistical Data):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 313):** Topic 9.1: Statistical Data
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 9.1: Statistical Data
> • Data Organization & Frequency Distributions: Discrete vs grouped frequency tables. Class intervals, lower/upper class boundaries, class mark (midpoint x = (L + U)/2), and cumulative frequency.
> • Graphical Data Representations: Bar charts (discrete categories, gaps between bars); Histograms (continuous data, bars touch, bar area proportional to frequency); Pie charts (circular sectors, sector angle = (f / N) × 360°).
> • Measures of Central Tendency: 1) Mean x̄ = (Σ x) / n or x̄ = (Σ f·x) / (Σ f); 2) Median: Middle score when data is ordered (for even n, average of two middle terms); 3) Mode: Most frequently occurring score (unimodal, bimodal, or no mode).
> • Basic Probability Concepts: Sample space S (all possible outcomes), Event E (subset of S). Theoretical Probability P(E) = n(E) / n(S) where 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. Complementary Event: P(E') = 1 - P(E).

---

### 📄 Textbook Page 322 — Structured Curriculum Text

## Unit 9: Statistics and Probability

Pie-charts

Data can be displayed on a pie chart-a circle divided into sectors. The size of the

sector is in direct proportion to the frequency of the

data. The sector size does not show the actual

frequency. The actual frequency can be calculated

easily from the size of the sector.

In a survey of 120 children, they were asked to choose their favorite color. The total

120 is represented by 100%. It follows that if 120 represent 100%, then

a. 50% represents 120 ( 50

100) = 60 children whose favorite is white.

b. 30% represents 120 ( 30

100) = 36 children whose favorite is purple.

c. 20% represents 120 ( 20

100) = 24 children whose favorite is blue.

Methods to represent a frequency distribution:

Distributions and histograms

Data should be organized once it is collected so that it can be manageable. Data that

is not organized is called raw data.

organization that can be measured or observed and that varies among the people

or organization being studied. A variable typically will vary in two or more

categories or on a continuum of scores, and it can be measured.

The mean is essentially a model of your data set. It is the value that is most common.

value that produces the lowest amount of error from all other values in the data set.

# Unit 9: Statistics and Probability
## 9.1 Statistical Data
*Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook • Textbook Page 331 of 363 (PDF Page 343) • Grade 9 Mathematics — Official Ethiopian Curriculum*

---

> 🎯 **Core Curriculum Objectives & Key Takeaways (9.1 Statistical Data):**
> • **Topic Focus (Starts on Textbook Page 313):** Topic 9.1: Statistical Data
> • Curriculum Focus: Topic 9.1: Statistical Data
> • Data Organization & Frequency Distributions: Discrete vs grouped frequency tables. Class intervals, lower/upper class boundaries, class mark (midpoint x = (L + U)/2), and cumulative frequency.
> • Graphical Data Representations: Bar charts (discrete categories, gaps between bars); Histograms (continuous data, bars touch, bar area proportional to frequency); Pie charts (circular sectors, sector angle = (f / N) × 360°).
> • Measures of Central Tendency: 1) Mean x̄ = (Σ x) / n or x̄ = (Σ f·x) / (Σ f); 2) Median: Middle score when data is ordered (for even n, average of two middle terms); 3) Mode: Most frequently occurring score (unimodal, bimodal, or no mode).
> • Basic Probability Concepts: Sample space S (all possible outcomes), Event E (subset of S). Theoretical Probability P(E) = n(E) / n(S) where 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. Complementary Event: P(E') = 1 - P(E).

---

### 📖 Structured AI Concept Breakdown & Explanation

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Statistics and probability provide tools for analyzing data and quantifying uncertainty. Descriptive statistics condense large data sets into summary averages and charts, while probability models chance events.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Topic 9.1: Statistical Data

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: In a histogram, bars MUST touch because data is continuous; in a bar chart, gaps separate discrete categories.
- **Key Principle**: The sum of sector angles in a pie chart is ALWAYS 360°.
- **Probability is strictly bounded**: Probability is strictly bounded: 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 (0 = impossible event, 1 = certain event).

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Data Central Tendency Distributions: Symmetric Distribution (Mean = Median = Mode) ──> Positively Skewed (Mode < Median < Mean) ──> Negatively Skewed (Mean < Median < Mode).
```

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Agricultural crop yield forecasting and national health epidemic tracking by the Ethiopian Public Health Institute rely on statistical measures and probability models.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
High-frequency EUEE questions: calculating mean of grouped frequency data, calculating pie chart sector angles, finding median from cumulative frequency, and calculating basic event probabilities.

experiments. Repeating the experiment sufficientely large number of times, however,

the relative frequency of an outcome will tend to be close to the theoretical

probability of that outcome.

i. If the event was tails, how many times did this event occur?

ii. According to the experiment, what was the probability of tails?

observation is recorded as follows:

Number of tosses Total

The number of times the coin is tossed 3 6 9 12 30

The number of times the coin shows up heads 1 4 4 6 15

The number of times the coin shows up tails 2 2 5 6 15

What proportion of the number of tosses shows Heads? Tails? What is the

probability that the outcome is Head? Tail?
